reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: The hallmark is sharp inferior heel pain that is worst with the first few steps in the morning or after periods of rest, then eases with activity
Tenderness is maximal at the medial calcaneal tubercle where the plantar fascia originates
It is a degenerative fasciopathy from repetitive overload rather than a primarily inflammatory condition, despite the -itis suffix
Risk factors include obesity, prolonged standing, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, tight calf muscles, and a sudden increase in running load
Diagnosis is clinical; a windlass test reproducing pain on passive great-toe dorsiflexion supports it
Heel spurs seen on radiographs are common incidental findings and do not cause the pain
Management principles are calf and plantar fascia stretching, load management, supportive footwear, and orthoses or heel cushioning
Most cases resolve within a year with conservative care; corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief but risks fat-pad atrophy and fascial rupture
Persistent bilateral heel pain, especially in a young person with inflammatory features, should prompt consideration of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy
reference.pathophysiology: Plantar fasciitis results from repetitive traction overload at the origin of the plantar aponeurosis on the medial calcaneal tuberosity. The tissue undergoes microtearing and a degenerative response with collagen disorganisation, mucoid change, and thickening of the fascia rather than sustained acute inflammation. Impaired ankle dorsiflexion and tight gastrocsoleus increase tensile strain, and the failed healing perpetuates pain.
additionalDifferentials: Tarsal tunnel syndrome or entrapment of the nerve to abductor digiti minimi (Baxter's nerve)
S1 radiculopathy referring to the heel
Insertional Achilles or retrocalcaneal pathology (posterior heel)
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to demonstrate a thickened, hypoechoic proximal plantar fascia
MRI in atypical or refractory cases and to exclude calcaneal stress fracture or nerve entrapment
Plain radiographs to identify a calcaneal stress fracture or other bony pathology
Inflammatory screen and referral if a spondyloarthropathy is suspected
redFlags: Features suggesting inflammatory arthropathy such as young age, bilateral disease, and other enthesitis or back symptoms
Focal bony tenderness or night pain raising concern for stress fracture or tumour
Numbness, tingling, or a positive Tinel sign suggesting nerve entrapment
Systemic symptoms or signs of infection
reference.prognosis: The large majority of patients improve within six to twelve months with conservative treatment, though symptoms can be protracted; recalcitrant cases may benefit from extracorporeal shockwave therapy before considering surgery.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to an incidental heel spur
Overusing corticosteroid injection with risk of fat-pad atrophy or fascial rupture
Missing a calcaneal stress fracture or nerve entrapment presenting as heel pain
Overlooking an underlying inflammatory spondyloarthropathy in bilateral or young patients
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Activity and load modification with relative rest from aggravating weight-bearing
Plantar fascia and gastrocsoleus stretching with calf-strengthening exercises through physiotherapy
Supportive footwear with cushioned heel cups or arch-supporting orthoses
Night splints to maintain dorsiflexion and reduce first-step morning pain
Simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptom relief
Corticosteroid injection reserved for refractory pain, used cautiously given the rupture risk
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for recalcitrant cases before considering surgery
Weight reduction and addressing contributory factors, with surgical release only as a last resort
